summary: Clarifies which IPv6 source address to use for Multicast Listener Discovery messages when a node is still performing stateless address autoconfiguration. It fixes an issue that came to light after earlier rules. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A computer joining a network may not have its address yet but still needs to speak up. This memo clears up what return address it may use.

questions: what is mld source address selection
why does mld use the unspecified address
subtitle: Lets IPv6 nodes send MLD Reports from the unspecified address while they are still checking their own link-local address.

tldr.problem: MLD required a link-local source address, but a node doing duplicate address detection has none yet. Some implementations skipped the MLD Reports, which broke MLD snooping switches.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3590 allows MLD Report and Done messages to use the unspecified address (::) as source when no valid link-local address exists. Queries must still use a link-local source, and routers discard Reports and Done messages from ::.
tldr.outcome: The document updates RFC 2710 as a Proposed Standard, so snooping switches can learn about duplicate address detection groups before the address is used.

today: RFC 3590 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2710, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the clarification of which source address MLD Report and Done messages may use before a link-local address is ready.

sections.title: The Conflict Between MLD and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
The original Multicast Listener Discovery specification (RFC 2710) says that MLD messages must use a link-local IPv6 source address. It also requires a node to send an MLD Report when it joins any IPv6 multicast group, except the All-Nodes address and addresses of scope less than 2.

That clashes with stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 2462). To perform duplicate address detection, a node has to join several multicast groups, but its only address is tentative and cannot be used for communication. It therefore has no suitable source address. RFC 3590 clarifies the source address rules for MLD when no link-local address is available.
sections.eli5: MLD says to write your return address on every note, but a new computer is still checking whether its address is free. It has nothing to write.

sections.title: Why the Rules Needed Fixing
sections.content:
Section 3 of RFC 2710 requires all MLD messages to carry a valid link-local source address. A node in the middle of duplicate address detection (DAD) for its link-local address does not have one. The RFC therefore allows the unspecified address as the source for MLD messages used during DAD.

The mismatch had caused real implementation problems. Several IPv6 implementations skipped sending MLD Reports during DAD because they had no valid link-local address. With switches that perform MLD snooping, DAD could then finish successfully while the switches had not forwarded the DAD messages to all nodes on the link. Address collisions could then occur once the address was in use.
sections.eli5: If a switch never hears you are interested in a group, it will not pass you those messages. Then you cannot hear if someone else already has your address.

sections.title: Source Address Selection Rules
sections.content:
An MLD node must pick a source address for all MLD messages: Report, Done and Query. The rules differ by message.

  • Query: MUST be sent with a valid link-local source address. A node (router or host) that receives a Query with source :: MUST silently discard it and SHOULD log a warning.
  • Report and Done: use a link-local source if a valid one is available on the interface. If not, for example because none has been configured, the message is sent with the unspecified address ::.

Once a valid link-local address is available, a node SHOULD generate new MLD Reports for all multicast addresses joined on the interface. Routers that receive a Report or Done with source :: MUST silently discard the packet without acting on its contents. Snooping switches MUST manage multicast forwarding state based on such Reports and Done messages.
sections.eli5: A question to the group needs a real return address. A plain I am here or I am leaving note may use a blank one, but routers ignore those, and the switches in the middle pay attention.

sections.title: Effects on Existing RFC 2710 Implementations
sections.content:
This memo adds to the RFC 2710 rule by allowing Report and Done messages to carry ::. How an RFC 2710 implementation reacts to such a message depends on how it treats the unspecified address. If it does not count the unspecified address as link-local in scope, it will drop the packets.

That is usually harmless, because the unspecified address is used only when there is no link-local address, so it should only be for joining the link-local solicited-node multicast group. A sender that joins other multicast groups before its link-local address is active could suffer a temporary black hole, since Reports from :: may be dropped. The gap lasts until the node can send a Report with a valid link-local address.
sections.eli5: Some older computers ignore notes with a blank return address. That is fine for this job, and anything missed is fixed as soon as the computer gets a real address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 2710 for the general security issues of MLD. For hosts and routers, all received MLD messages from an unspecified source address are silently discarded, which is the required behavior from RFC 2710 and is not changed here. The RFC concludes that the changes have no new security impacts.

Snooping switches, however, now keep multicast forwarding state based on Report and Done messages sent from the unspecified address. The RFC says the vulnerabilities in that case are similar to those for forged messages, which RFC 2710 describes in its security considerations section.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky for computers and routers, since they ignore blank-address notes. The switches do act on them, so someone could fake a note, much like before.
